area: Area VII. Slow Flight and Stalls
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a stalled, yawing airplane spins, name and recognize the entry, incipient, developed and recovery phases, give the POH and AFH spin recovery steps in order, and identify the loading, control and flight situations that turn an ordinary stall into an inadvertent spin.
why: An airplane must be stalled and yawed to spin, and mishandled yaw in a stall is what usually starts one [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Stall and spin accidents were found to be about one quarter of fatal general aviation accidents, and most began with a pilot who was briefly distracted from flying [[13:4|AC 61-67C para 3]]. Spin awareness is a knowledge and risk task with no flight skills to demonstrate, so your examiner tests it by asking and by watching how you avoid the setups (ACS CA.VII.E).

prereading.what: Spin awareness, what causes a spin, the four phases, the six-step recovery template, intentional spins and placards, weight and balance, spin errors, and the spiral dive. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 5-22 to 5-27

prereading.what: Accelerated stalls and the cross-control stall, including the skidding base-to-final turn.
prereading.label: AFH 5-19 to 5-20

prereading.what: Stall and spin definitions, weight, CG, turbulence, distractions, stall recognition, primary cause of spins, spin types, recovery and the spiral mode.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C, Ch 1 (para 100 to 112)

prereading.what: Who must take spin training, parachutes, how normal, utility and acrobatic airplanes were spin tested, and spin placards.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C, Ch 3 to 4 (para 300 to 402)

prereading.what: Effect of weight and load distribution, aft CG and spin recovery, and the flat spin.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-42 to 5-44

prereading.what: Stall recognition by sight, sound and feel, when the published stall speed is valid, and AOA indicator limits.
prereading.label: AFH 5-13 to 5-14

prereading.what: Task saturation, missing warnings, spatial disorientation, and surprise and startle.
prereading.label: AFH 5-3

warmup: Think first: two wings on the same airplane, both past the critical angle of attack. One is going down and one is coming up. Which one meets the air at a steeper angle, which one makes more drag, and what does that difference do to the airplane once it starts to turn? Hold your answer until chunk 3.

key_terms.def: An aggravated stall that results in autorotation: the airplane follows a downward corkscrew path while rolling, yawing and pitching [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 107]] [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

The self-sustaining rotation of a spin. The descending wing is more stalled than the rising wing, which keeps the airplane rotating around a vertical axis [[24:386|AFH G-14]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 107]].
The one angle of attack at which a given wing stalls. It does not change with weight, bank, temperature, density altitude or CG [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]].
The pilot, on purpose or by accident, provides what a spin needs: a stall plus yaw [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
From the stall and start of rotation until the spin is fully developed; forces are not yet in balance. Two to four turns in most airplanes [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
Rotation rate, airspeed and vertical speed are stable and the path is nearly vertical; the spin is in equilibrium [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 110]].
A spin with a near-level pitch and roll attitude and the spin axis near the CG. Recovery may be extremely difficult or impossible [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 110]].
A nose-low, descending turn in which the airplane is not stalled, so airspeed and G-load build rapidly [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
A stall with aileron one way and rudder the other; it can roll the airplane toward inverted, often the start of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
A stall caused by hurrying the recovery before the airplane has regained enough flying speed [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 106]].
An older certification category intended for limited acrobatic operation; its limit load factor is 4.4 to -1.76 [[24:388|AFH G-16]] [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].
At a high AOA the downward-moving blade (normally on the right) makes more thrust, so the airplane tends to yaw left [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

body.p: The objective is knowledge of what causes unintentional spins, how to recover, and the risks that go with them (ACS CA.VII.E Objective). There are three knowledge elements: spin aerodynamics in various configurations, including angle of attack, airspeed, load factor, power, weight and CG, attitude and yaw (K1); what causes a spin and how to identify the entry, incipient and developed phases (K2); and the recovery procedure (K3).

head: Element

How AOA, airspeed, load factor, power, weight and CG, attitude and yaw affect spins in different configurations
K2

K3 and R3
The spin recovery procedure: POH first, AFH template if there is none
R1 to R6

Skills

body.p: Table source: ACS CA.VII.E. The private ACS Task (PA.VII.D) lists the same K1 to K3 and R1 to R6 elements, word for word, and also leaves Skills blank. So the difference at commercial level is depth, not new elements: you are expected to explain the why, link it to loading and operating limits, and show it in how you fly every other Task.

callout.text: Stall and spin awareness applies to the whole test. The applicant and the evaluator must always recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin (ACS Appendix 2, Stall and Spin Awareness).
Bring your POH spin section to the oral. The AFH says the POH techniques take precedence over its generic ones [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

check.q: Will you be asked to fly a spin on the commercial ASEL practical test?
check.a: No. The Skills section of CA.VII.E is intentionally left blank; the Task is tested on knowledge and risk management (ACS CA.VII.E).

chunks.title: Stalled plus yawed: what makes a spin

body.p: A spin is an aggravated stall. The airplane follows a downward corkscrew path, rotating about a vertical axis while it rolls, yaws and pitches. In every spin at least one wing is stalled [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. All spins are preceded by a stall on at least part of the wing [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100]].

The recipe has two ingredients: at least one wing past the critical AOA, and a sideslip or yaw acting on the airplane at or beyond the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Remove either one and there is no spin. That is why the AFH says the airplane must be stalled and yawed to spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

Where does the yaw come from? Not only from wrong rudder. The AFH also lists adverse yaw from aileron, engine and propeller effects (P-factor, torque, spiraling slipstream, gyroscopic precession), and wind shear, including wake turbulence [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. The AC names the primary cause of an inadvertent spin as exceeding the critical AOA while using too much or too little rudder and, to a lesser extent, aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

The stall itself is about AOA, not speed. A stall can happen at any airspeed, in any attitude, with any power setting [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100]]. A given airplane always stalls at the same critical AOA; what changes is the airspeed at which you get there [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

callout.text: No stall, no spin. No yaw, no spin. Break the stall and stop the yaw.
Keeping the nose from yawing before you start stall recovery is the key to averting a spin. Use the right amount of rudder to stop the yaw and keep the wings from banking [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

check.q: Name the two things that must both be present for a spin.
check.a: A stall (at least one wing past the critical AOA) and yaw or sideslip at or beyond the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

body.p: As the airplane rotates, the rising wing is less stalled than the descending wing. The difference creates the rolling, yawing and pitching motion of the spin [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 107]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 107]]. Each wing has different lift and drag forces acting on it [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

Look at the close-up on the left of Figure 5-16. The descending wing meets the relative wind at a greater AOA, is more stalled, and has less lift and more drag. The rising wing has a smaller AOA, is less stalled, and has more lift and less drag [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. Application: more lift on the rising side keeps rolling the airplane toward the low wing, and more drag on the low wing keeps yawing it the same way. The motion feeds itself, which is what autorotation means.

Inside a developed spin the numbers are not what most pilots expect. Airspeed is very low, usually within 2 knots of the unaccelerated stall speed, and the load factor is usually only slightly above 1 G, because the airplane pivots rather than turns [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. The indicated airspeed should be low and constant, not climbing [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

The loads come later. Spin recoveries are made with the nose much lower than stall recoveries, so airspeed and load factor in the pull-out are higher; a proper spin recovery usually runs about 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor, so a hard pull can stall the airplane again at a high airspeed [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100g]].

callout.text: If the airspeed is increasing, you are no longer in a spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. A fast-building airspeed in a steep, rotating descent means a spiral, which has a different recovery (chunk 6).

check.q: In a spin, which wing has the greater AOA and more drag?
check.a: The descending wing; it is more stalled than the rising wing [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 107]].

chunks.title: The four phases of a spin

body.p: The AFH divides a spin into entry, incipient, developed and recovery [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

head: Phase
What is happening
How you recognize it
rows: Entry

The pilot, on purpose or by accident, supplies the stall and the yaw. An intentional entry is like a power-off stall with full rudder toward the spin and full back elevator at the stall [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Stall cues plus a yaw you did not stop
Incipient
Stalled and rotating; aerodynamic and inertial forces not yet balanced. Two to four turns in most airplanes [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Airspeed settling low and steady; the turn indicator's symbolic airplane shows the spin direction [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Developed
Rotation rate, airspeed and vertical speed stable; path nearly vertical; forces in balance [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
A steady, repeating rotation
Recovery
Rotation stops and the wings' AOA drops below critical. A quarter turn to several turns, depending on airplane and spin type [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Rotation slowing, then airspeed rising as the wing unstalls [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]

body.p: Begin incipient spin recovery before 360 degrees of rotation, with full rudder opposite the rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. The earlier you act, the less altitude and the fewer turns it takes.

Do not use the ball to find the spin direction. Where the instrument is mounted decides which way the ball goes; a ball on the left side of the panel moves left even in a spin to the right. Use the turn indicator, which deflects toward the rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

Some training airplanes never reach a developed spin. They can slide out of the incipient phase into a spiral dive, which is not in equilibrium: it accelerates, and G-load can build fast [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

callout.text: Entry: stalled plus yaw. Incipient: turning but not settled. Developed: settled and steady. Recovery: rotation stops, wing unstalls.

check.q: During an incipient spin the ball is pinned to the left. Is the spin to the left?
check.a: Not necessarily. The ball's position depends on where the instrument is mounted; use the turn indicator for direction [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

chunks.title: Spin recovery: POH first, then the AFH template

body.p: Always follow the manufacturer's recovery procedure. Use the AFH six-step template only when the manufacturer gives none [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. If flaps or retractable gear were out before the spin, retract them as soon as practicable after spin entry [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

head: Step
Why (AFH)
rows: 1. Power to idle
Power aggravates spin characteristics: a flatter attitude and usually a faster rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
2. Ailerons neutral
Aileron with the spin can speed the rotation and delay recovery; aileron against the spin can flatten it, delay recovery, or even make it unrecoverable [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
3. Full opposite rudder, held until rotation stops
Rudder is usually the most important recovery control in single-engine airplanes. Brisk and full; slow, cautious rudder can let it keep spinning [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
4. Positive, brisk, straight forward elevator (forward of neutral)
Right after the rudder; do not wait for rotation to stop. Lowers AOA and drives the wing toward unstalled flight; some airplanes need full forward [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
5. Neutralize rudder when rotation stops
Leaving it in as speed builds causes yawing or sideslip [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
6. Back elevator to level flight, adjust power
Not too much: excess back pressure can cause a secondary stall and another spin. Stay inside G and airspeed limits [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]

callout.text: PARE: Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder full opposite, Elevator brisk forward. Then neutralize the rudder and pull out gently. PARE is a common instructor memory aid, not an FAA term; it covers AFH steps 1 to 4 only.

body.p: The AC adds two practical points. Assume power may not be available: in a spin, centrifugal force on the fuel can interrupt it and stop the engine [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]]. And some airplanes need only a relaxation of back pressure while others need full forward elevator, which is one more reason the POH comes first [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]].

callout.text: Wrong rudder is the fastest way to lose the recovery. Find the direction from the outside view and the turn indicator, not the ball [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

check.q: After full opposite rudder, when does the forward elevator go in?
check.a: Immediately after the rudder, briskly. Do not wait for the rotation to stop [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

chunks.title: After the rotation: secondary stalls and the spiral trap

body.p: The pull-out is where many recoveries go wrong. Hurrying the recovery before the airplane has regained flying speed causes a secondary stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 106]]. Too much or too abrupt back pressure, or rudder and aileron during the recovery, can stall it again and possibly start another spin [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]].

A spin and a spiral dive can look alike from inside: nose low, turning, losing altitude. The airspeed tells them apart. In a spin the wing is stalled and the airspeed is low and steady. In a spiral the airplane is not stalled, so the airspeed and G-load build rapidly [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. A spin can also degenerate into a spiral as the nose goes more vertical [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 112]].

bullets: 1. Power to idle, to slow the acceleration [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
2. Some forward elevator to unload to about 1 G before rolling. This prevents a rolling pull-out, where the design limit is exceeded more easily [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
3. Roll wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
4. Gently raise the nose to level flight; you may be at or beyond VNE [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
5. Once at VY, add climb power and climb to a safe altitude [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

callout.text: The startled response to a spiral is to pull back hard while rolling level. That can cause structural damage or failure [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
Spin: airspeed low and steady, use rudder. Spiral: airspeed racing, use power off, unload, roll, then pull gently.

check.q: You apply spin recovery, and the airspeed is now climbing fast with the nose low and banked. What is happening?
check.a: You are no longer spinning; it is a spiral. Use the spiral recovery: power idle, unload, roll level, gently raise the nose [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

chunks.title: Weight, CG and the flat spin

body.p: Even minor weight or balance changes can change spin and recovery behavior, for better or worse. Extra weight in the aft baggage compartment, or extra fuel, may still be inside CG limits and still seriously affect the spin and its recovery [[24:131|AFH 5-26]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 108]].

Aft CG is the big one. As the CG moves aft, less elevator is needed to stall at a given load factor, so inadvertent stalls are easier to enter and higher load factors are easier to pull in the recovery [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100h]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100h]]. Recovery from a stall gets progressively harder as the CG moves aft [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]. An airplane that recovers cleanly from a prolonged spin may fail to respond to normal recovery inputs with the CG one or two inches further aft [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]].

Far enough aft, a flat spin develops. Centrifugal force acting through the aft CG swings the tail out away from the spin axis, so the nose cannot be brought down [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]]. The attitude is nearly level in pitch and roll, with the spin axis near the CG, and recovery is often impossible [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100h]] [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 110]].

Forward CG works the other way: the stall comes at a higher airspeed and needs more back pressure [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100h]] [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]]. Heavier weight raises the stall speed because a higher AOA is needed to support the weight [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100i]].

callout.text: In one two-seat trainer, no baggage at all may be carried aft of the seats when spins are to be practiced [[1:139|PHAK 5-42]]. Commercial flying often means full seats and bags: run the weight and balance, and treat a loading near the aft limit as a less spin-forgiving airplane.

check.q: Why does an aft CG make a flat spin more likely?
check.a: Centrifugal force acting through the aft CG pulls the tail out from the spin axis so the nose cannot be lowered to recover [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

chunks.title: Spin types: what flattens, speeds up or changes a spin

body.p: The spin types an airplane shows depend on its design, its loading, the control inputs and the density altitude [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. The FAA sources name these:

head: Type
Description
Source
rows: Incipient
From the stall and start of rotation until fully developed
Fully developed (steady state)
Rotation rate, airspeed and vertical speed stable turn to turn, path close to vertical
Flat
Near-level pitch and roll, spin axis near the CG; recovery may be extremely difficult or impossible
Spiral mode
Autorotation similar to a spin, center of rotation near the centerline, but not stalled

body.p: Things that make a spin faster or flatter, from the AFH: power gives a flatter attitude and usually faster rotation; aileron with the spin speeds the rotation and steepens the attitude; aileron against the spin can flatten it [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Aft CG and extra weight push toward the flat spin (chunk 7).

Spins from accelerated stalls: a stall at more than 1 G comes at a higher airspeed, is usually more severe, and often surprises the pilot [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]]. An accelerated stall can put the airplane in an unexpected attitude, and failure to recover at once may result in a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Application: a spin entered this way starts with more energy and more abruptly than the slow, power-off entry pilots picture.

Configuration: flaps change the stall speed [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100]], and accelerated stalls should never be practiced with flaps out because of their lower G limits [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. If flaps or retractable gear are out when a spin starts, retract them as soon as practicable [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

callout.text: 'Accelerated spin' is a hangar term; none of the FAA sources used here defines it. On the oral, stick to the source descriptions above and say what makes rotation faster (power, pro-spin aileron) and what makes the attitude flatter (power, aft CG, anti-spin aileron).

check.q: Name two pilot inputs that can flatten a spin.
check.a: Power left on, and aileron held against the spin direction [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

chunks.title: Approved for spins? Categories, placards and rules

body.p: If the manufacturer does not approve an airplane for spins, intentional spins are not authorized. The official sources are the Type Certificate Data Sheet or aircraft specifications, the AFM/POH limitations section, and a placard in clear view of the pilot [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

head: Legacy category
Spin testing
Typical placard
rows: Normal
Recover from a one-turn or 3-second spin, whichever is longer, in no more than one additional turn [[13:21|AC 61-67C para 400]]
No acrobatic maneuvers, including spins, approved [[13:22|AC 61-67C para 401]]
Utility
Meets normal and acrobatic spin requirements if approved for spins [[13:22|AC 61-67C para 400]]
Lists approved maneuvers, or says spins prohibited [[13:22|AC 61-67C para 401]]
Acrobatic
Recover from up to six turns in no more than one and a half additional turns [[13:21|AC 61-67C para 400]]
Lists approved maneuvers and recovery control actions [[13:22|AC 61-67C para 401]]

body.p: Normal-category airplanes certified under the older 14 CFR 23.221(a) only had to recover from a one-turn or 3-second spin (or show spin resistance), so many were never required to recover from a fully developed spin. In any airplane placarded against spins, there is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin; assume it could become uncontrollable [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Today's 14 CFR 23.2150 requires single-engine airplanes not certified for aerobatics to have no tendency to inadvertently depart controlled flight [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]], and allows them maneuvers incident to normal flying, including stalls (except whip stalls) and steep turns up to 60 degrees of bank [[60:99|14 CFR 23.2005]].

The utility trap: an airplane approved for spins in the utility category usually has an aft CG limit several inches forward of the normal-category limit [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]. Loaded to normal-category limits it can enter a spin more easily and may not recover from one that goes beyond one turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

callout.text: With anyone aboard who is not a crewmember, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees nose up or down unless every occupant wears an approved parachute. Exceptions: flight tests for a certificate or rating, and spins and other required maneuvers given by a CFI (or an ATP instructing under 61.67) [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].

Spin training is required only for flight instructor airplane and glider applicants [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183(i)]] [[13:19|AC 61-67C para 300]]. As a commercial pilot you may never have spun an airplane; if you go on to CFI, you will.

check.q: Where do you look to learn whether your airplane is approved for spins?
check.a: The Type Certificate Data Sheet or specifications, the AFM/POH limitations section, and the placard in view of the pilot [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

body.p: The classic: a skidding turn from base to final. A tailwind on base raises the groundspeed, the pilot turns late or too shallow, and overshoots the centerline. To fix it the pilot steepens the bank, adds back pressure and pushes inside rudder to swing the nose around. The bank tries to increase, the nose slices down, the pilot pulls, the AOA reaches critical, and the airplane can snap into a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

In a cross-controlled stall the spin usually goes the way the rudder is pushed, whichever wingtip is up [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. In a skid (aileron and rudder the same way) it rotates in the direction of the controls; in a slip (aileron held against rudder) it usually goes opposite the aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

head: Setup
What goes wrong
Source
rows: Base-to-final overshoot
Skidding, cross-controlled turn near the ground
Go-around or short-field takeoff
High pitch, high power, low speed; too little or too much rudder for P-factor
Go-around with nose-up trim
Pitch rises sharply and yaws left as power comes in
High sink rate on final
Trying to stop it with pitch alone
Steep turn with nose dropping
Raising the nose without shallowing the bank tightens the turn toward a diving spiral
Uncoordinated slow flight
Mishandled controls in turns, stalls and slow flight spin even reluctant airplanes

callout.text: The safest fix for an overshoot is a go-around. Low on base-to-final, be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees and never skid the turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Low altitude multiplies the danger. More than 25 percent of general aviation fatal accidents happen in the maneuvering phase, and half of those involve stall or spin [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. Unnecessary low flying and impromptu demonstrations for people on the ground can push a pilot past their capabilities [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

check.q: Base to final, you hold left aileron and push right rudder (a slip) and the airplane stalls. Which way does it likely spin?
check.a: To the right: in a slipping turn the spin usually goes opposite the aileron, which is the direction of the rudder [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]] [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

body.p: Many airplanes have stall warning devices that alert you 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 103]]. Certification allows the warning to come from the airplane's own pre-stall buffet instead of a device, and most vintage airplanes and many light-sport and experimental airplanes have no device at all [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

The published 1 G stall speed is valid only in unaccelerated 1 G flight, coordinated, at one weight (usually maximum), and at one CG (usually most forward) [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Change any of those and the stall moves. Bank is the big one in the pattern.

In a level 60 degree bank the load factor is 2 G and the stall speed is about 40 percent higher [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100]]. Stall speed grows with the square root of the load factor: an airplane that stalls at 45 knots unaccelerated stalls at 90 knots at 4 G [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100g]].

bullets: A stall warning system can fail; then buffet, loss of roll authority or an inability to stop a descent are your cues [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
With ice or other contamination, the stall may come with little or none of the usual cues, at a lower AOA and a higher airspeed [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 102]].

In uncoordinated flight the pitot-static instruments, especially airspeed and altitude, are unreliable, so you may not know the critical AOA is near until the warning sounds [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].
AOA indicators help but have limits: calibration, unheated probes, the type of indicator, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].
Sight, sound and feel still matter: lighter controls, a change in the airflow sound, and seat-of-the-pants sensations [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

callout.text: The warning tells you the stall is near; it does not tell you whether a spin is near. A stall warning plus yaw is the moment to reduce AOA and stop the yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

check.q: List the four conditions under which the published 1 G stall speed is valid.
check.a: Unaccelerated 1 G flight, coordinated, at one weight, and at one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

body.p: Turbulence can stall an airplane at a much higher airspeed than in smooth air: a vertical gust or wind shear suddenly raises the AOA. In moderate to severe turbulence, fly well above the stall speed and below maneuvering speed, remembering that maneuvering speed is lower at a lower weight [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100l]].

A microburst is the most severe low-level wind shear. Its downdrafts can reach 6,000 feet per minute, and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots can follow [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Application: a big, sudden AOA change close to the ground, while the pilot pulls to hold the path, is exactly the stalled plus yawed setup.

Density altitude barely changes the indicated stall speed, but it raises the true airspeed and cuts performance [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100j]]. The spin type an airplane shows can depend on density altitude [[24:127|AFH 5-22]], and altitude losses in a spin are greater at higher density altitude [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]].

Altitude budget: the AFH says the first turn of a spin loses about 1,000 feet and each later turn about half that [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. The AC gives about 500 feet for each 3-second turn in most small airplanes approved for spins [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]]. Intentional spins should begin high enough to finish recovery at or above 1,500 feet AGL [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

Collision hazards: a spin drops you through other airplanes' altitudes in seconds. Before any intentional spin, clear the area above and below you [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. Scan in short movements of no more than 10 degrees, each held for at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

callout.text: Gusty day, hot day, heavy airplane: carry a little more speed on approach in gusts or strong crosswinds [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100l]], and keep pattern turns coordinated and no steeper than about 30 degrees [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

check.q: Using the AFH rule, about how much altitude does a two-turn spin take before recovery begins?
check.a: About 1,500 feet: 1,000 for the first turn plus about 500 for the second [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

body.p: NTSB data show most stall and spin accidents happen when the pilot is distracted for a moment from flying [[13:4|AC 61-67C para 3]]. Typical distractions: finding a checklist, trying an engine restart, a windy traffic pattern, reading a chart, working fuel or distance numbers, or reaching for something on the floor or in the back seat [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 101]].

That is why the evaluator is told to add realistic distractions during the flight test and watch your situational awareness and control while you divide your attention (ACS Appendix 2, Use of Distractions).

Upsets bring their own trouble. Startle is an automatic reflex to a sudden, intense event that violates your expectations; untrained pilots often experience surprise or startle in an upset. Scenario-based training with realistic distractions helps protect against it [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Spatial disorientation is a factor in many upsets, and a disoriented pilot may not know it [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

bullets: Fly first: when a stall warning comes during a distraction, drop the task and reduce AOA.
In a spin, read rotation from the outside view and the turn indicator, not the ball [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
Expect an unusual feel: in a spin the load factor is only a little over 1 G and airspeed is near the stall [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].
UPRT skills are perishable; recurrent practice keeps them [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

callout.text: Distraction + low speed + uncoordinated = spin setup. Aviate first.

check.q: Give three distractions the AC lists as common in stall accidents.
check.a: Any three of: locating a checklist, an engine restart, a windy traffic pattern, reading a chart, fuel or distance calculations, retrieving items from the floor, back seat or glove box [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 101]].

body.p: The AFH lists these errors for intentional spins. Most of them are also how an inadvertent spin recovery fails [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

head: AFH common error
What happens
Fix
rows: Not enough rudder against the spin, or applied slowly
Rotation continues, maybe indefinitely
Full rudder to the stop, briskly [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Not enough forward elevator
Wing stays stalled
Positive, brisk forward elevator, full if the POH says so [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Waiting for rotation to stop before forward elevator
Longer recovery, more altitude
Forward elevator right after the rudder [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Rudder not neutralized after rotation stops
Yaw or sideslip, possibly a secondary spin
Neutralize as soon as rotation stops [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Too much back elevator after rotation stops
Secondary stall, possibly another spin
Smooth pull, within G limits [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Too little back elevator
Excessive airspeed
Steady pull-out once the rudder is neutral [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Slow, overly cautious inputs
The spin keeps going
Brisk, positive control movement [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]

body.p: Table source: [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]; fixes as cited.

Errors that cause the spin in the first place, from the stall error list: pulling too fast on entry and getting an accelerated stall, losing coordination, leveling the wings or adding power before reducing AOA, and a secondary stall in the recovery [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

callout.text: In a spiral, the errors are the opposite family: not reducing power, adding power, pulling out without rolling level, pulling and rolling at the same time, and not unloading first [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

check.q: Rotation has just stopped. What two things must you do next, and what goes wrong if you overdo the second?
check.a: Neutralize the rudder, then apply back pressure to level flight. Too much back pressure can cause a secondary stall and another spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-15. Spin, an aggravated stall and autorotation. (AFH 5-22)
f1.alt: An airplane, nose down and banked, rotating around a tall vertical pole while following a yellow and brown ribbon that corkscrews down around the pole against a blue sky.

f2.caption: Figure 5-16. Spin entry and recovery. (AFH 5-23)
f2.alt: Left: an airplane in a spin with arrows on each wing. The rising wing is labeled less stalled, with a smaller angle of attack, a large lift arrow and a small drag arrow. The descending wing is labeled more stalled, with a greater angle of attack, a small lift arrow and a larger drag arrow. Right: a column with an airplane path stalling at the top and corkscrewing down through orange, red and green bands, with boxes: incipient spin, about 4 to 6 seconds and about 2 turns; fully developed spin, stabilized airspeed, vertical speed and rotation, about 500 feet lost per 3-second turn; recovery, wings regain lift, about one quarter to one half turn after anti-spin inputs.

f3.caption: Figure 5-17. Spin recovery template. (AFH 5-24)
f3.alt: A yellow table titled Spin Recovery Template with six rows: reduce power to idle; ailerons neutral; full opposite rudder against the rotation; positive, brisk, straight forward elevator, forward of neutral; neutralize rudder after rotation stops; back elevator to return to level flight and adjust power.

f4.caption: Figure 5-63. Effect of load distribution on balance. (PHAK 5-43)
f4.alt: Two side views of the same airplane. Top: forward CG ahead of the center of lift, with a stronger down load on the tail. Bottom: aft CG closer to the center of lift, with a lighter down load on the tail.

f5.caption: Figure 5-18. Spiral dive recovery template. (AFH 5-27)
f5.alt: A yellow table titled Spiral Dive Recovery Template with five rows: reduce power to idle; apply some forward elevator; roll wings level; gently raise the nose to level flight; increase power to climb power.

f6.caption: Figure 3-13. Indications of a slip and skid. (AFH 3-13)
f6.alt: Three panels: skid, coordinated turn and slip. Each shows an attitude indicator in a turn, a turn coordinator and a seat. Skid: ball to the outside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the outside. Coordinated: ball centered and the pilot pressed straight down. Slip: ball to the inside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the inside.

f7.caption: Figure 5-39. Increase in stall speed and load factor. (PHAK 5-26)
f7.alt: A graph against bank angle from 0 to 90 degrees. A red curve shows the percent increase in stall speed, from 0 at wings level, slowly rising, then shooting up past 100 percent near 77 degrees. A black curve shows load factor in G, from 1 at wings level, nearly flat to about 50 degrees, then rising steeply toward 13 G near 85 degrees.

scenario.title: A hot, gusty afternoon with a full airplane
scenario.setup: You are a new commercial pilot flying a four-seat trainer placarded 'No acrobatic maneuvers, including spins, approved.' Three passengers and their bags put the CG close to the aft limit. The field elevation is high and it is hot, with gusty winds. On downwind a passenger asks you to 'do something fun,' and on base you notice a strong tailwind pushing you toward the extended centerline.

questions.q: How does today's loading change the stall and spin picture?
questions.a: Near the aft limit, less elevator force is needed to stall, so an inadvertent stall is easier and higher loads are easier to pull in recovery [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100h]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100h]]. Spin recovery gets harder as the CG moves aft [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]. Heavier weight also raises the stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100i]].

questions.q: The passenger wants a steep, nose-low maneuver. What limits apply?
questions.a: With non-crew passengers and no parachutes, no intentional maneuver past 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees nose up or down [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. The placard prohibits spins, and in an airplane placarded against spins there is no assurance of recovery [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

questions.q: You overshoot the turn to final. What do you do, and what do you not do?
questions.a: Go around. Do not steepen the bank past about 30 degrees, and never push inside rudder to skid the nose around; that is the classic cross-control stall and spin setup [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: On the go-around the nose pitches up and yaws left as power comes in. Why is that a spin risk and what is the fix?
questions.a: High pitch, high power and low speed make P-factor strong; too little or too much rudder leaves you uncoordinated near the critical AOA [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]]. Nose-up trim adds to the pitch-up [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Hold the attitude with forward pressure, coordinate with right rudder, and retrim.

questions.q: Can you trust the stall horn today?
questions.a: Only as one cue. It normally sounds 4 to 8 knots early [[13:10|AC 61-67C para 103]], but in gusts the airplane can stall at a higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100l]], and in uncoordinated flight the airspeed indicator itself is unreliable [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]]. Use AOA, feel and sound too [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

questions.q: Suppose it did stall and start to rotate on climb-out at altitude. What do you do?
questions.a: Follow the POH spin recovery. Without one, the AFH template: power idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, brisk forward elevator, neutralize rudder when rotation stops, then pull out gently [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Expect large altitude loss, more at high density altitude [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]].

quiz.q: Besides wrong rudder, what does the AFH say can yaw an airplane at the stall and help start a spin?
options: Only an engine failure
Adverse yaw from aileron, engine and propeller effects, and wind shear including wake turbulence
Only flap or landing gear extension
Nothing else; rudder is the only source of yaw
quiz.why: The AFH lists adverse yaw from aileron deflection, engine and propeller effects (P-factor, torque, spiraling slipstream, gyroscopic precession), and wind shear including wake turbulence [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

quiz.q: In a spin, how does the descending wing compare with the rising wing?
options: It is less stalled and makes more lift
It is more stalled and at a greater AOA
Both wings are at exactly the same AOA
It is unstalled while the rising wing is stalled
quiz.why: The rising wing is less stalled than the descending wing; the descending wing is at a greater AOA with more drag [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 107]] [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

quiz.q: Why should you not use the slip-skid ball to find the direction of a spin?
options: It always reads backwards in a spin
Its movement depends on where the instrument is mounted, not on the rotation
It freezes at high G
It only works in a flat spin
quiz.why: The location of the instrument decides how the ball moves; a left-mounted ball moves left even in a right spin. Use the turn indicator [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH template start with the throttle to idle?
options: To keep the engine from overspeeding only
Power aggravates the spin: flatter attitude and usually faster rotation
To make the stall horn sound
Power has no effect; it is just tradition
quiz.why: Power aggravates spin characteristics, giving a flatter attitude and usually a higher rotation rate [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

quiz.q: During spin recovery, what can aileron held against the direction of the spin do?
options: Speed up the recovery
Flatten the spin and delay recovery, possibly making it unrecoverable
Nothing, ailerons are ineffective when stalled
Turn the spin into a spiral
quiz.why: Aileron opposite the spin may flatten it and delay recovery, or even cause an unrecoverable spin; neutral is best [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

quiz.q: Why is the aft CG limit for spins in the utility category usually further forward than the normal-category limit?
options: To save fuel
Spin recovery gets harder as the CG moves aft
To raise the stall speed for training
Utility airplanes have shorter wings
quiz.why: Designers set the utility spin aft limit several inches forward of the normal limit; recovery from a stall or spin gets harder as the CG moves aft [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]].

quiz.q: Under the older Part 23 placard rules quoted in AC 61-67C, what placard does a normal-category airplane carry?
options: 'Spins approved with flaps up only'
'No acrobatic maneuvers, including spins, approved'
'Acrobatic maneuvers limited to the following'
No placard is required
quiz.why: Normal-category airplanes must have a placard in clear view of the pilot stating 'No acrobatic maneuvers, including spins, approved' [[13:22|AC 61-67C para 401]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say helps protect a pilot against a debilitating surprise or startle response in an upset?
options: Turning off the stall warning to reduce noise
Scenario-based training with realistic distractions
Flying only with an autopilot
Avoiding all stall practice
quiz.why: Pilots can protect themselves through scenario-based training, where instructors add realistic distractions to provoke surprise or startle [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

quiz.q: How fast can microburst downdrafts be?
options: Up to about 600 fpm
Up to about 1,500 fpm
Up to about 6,000 fpm
Up to about 20,000 fpm
quiz.why: A microburst can produce downdrafts of up to 6,000 fpm [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

quiz.q: Which statement about a developed spin is correct?
options: Load factor is usually 3 to 4 G
Airspeed is usually within about 2 knots of the unaccelerated stall speed
The airplane is not stalled
Airspeed keeps increasing turn after turn
quiz.why: In a spin the airspeed is very low, usually within 2 knots of the unaccelerated stall speed, and load factor is only slightly above 1 G because the airplane pivots [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

final_quiz.q: You start spin recovery. The rotation seems to stop, but now the nose is steeply down, the bank is steep, and the airspeed is climbing through the yellow arc. What first?
options: Full back elevator to stop the descent
Power to idle, then some forward elevator to unload before rolling level
Full opposite rudder again
Add full power to recover altitude
final_quiz.why: Rising airspeed means you are no longer in a spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. It is a spiral: power idle, unload with some forward elevator, roll level, then gently raise the nose [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Pulling while rolling invites structural failure.

final_quiz.q: Your CFI demonstrates a spin in an approved airplane. After rotation stops, you keep holding full rudder as the speed builds. What is the likely result?
options: Nothing; it helps hold heading
Yawing or sideslip, possibly a secondary spin
A faster pull-out
The engine stops
final_quiz.why: Failing to neutralize the rudder when rotation stops causes yawing or sideslip and possibly a secondary spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: A friend says to hold full opposite rudder and wait until the rotation stops before moving the elevator. What does the AFH say?
options: Correct; elevator only after rotation stops
Apply brisk forward elevator immediately after the rudder; do not wait
Never move the elevator in a spin
Pull back to raise the nose first
final_quiz.why: Step 4 comes immediately after full rudder; waiting for rotation to stop is a listed common error [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: On preflight before a dual spin-training flight you find the rudder cable noticeably slack. Why does the AFH care?
options: It only affects taxi steering
Slack rudder or elevator cables could prevent full anti-spin deflection and delay or prevent recovery
It makes the stall horn inaccurate
It moves the CG aft
final_quiz.why: Slack or loose control cables, particularly rudder and elevator, could prevent full anti-spin control deflections and delay or preclude recovery in some airplanes [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

final_quiz.q: Your CFI tries to demonstrate a spin with the CG well forward. Instead of settling into a spin, the nose drops further and the airspeed builds quickly. What happened?
options: A flat spin developed
The airplane went into a spiral; many airplanes will not spin at a forward CG but will spiral
A normal developed spin; airspeed always rises in a spin
A secondary stall
final_quiz.why: Many airplanes will not spin at forward CG locations but will spiral; in the spiral the airspeed increases and recovery must be immediate [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 112]]. A spiral is recognized by rapidly increasing airspeed after the attempted entry [[13:19|AC 61-67C para 300]].

final_quiz.q: You inadvertently stall and start to spin with flaps at 20 degrees on a go-around. What does the AFH say about the flaps?
options: Leave them until on the ground
Retract them as soon as practicable after spin entry
Extend them fully to slow down
Retract them only after reaching VY
final_quiz.why: If flaps or retractable gear are extended before the spin, retract them as soon as practicable after spin entry [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Your POH procedure governs if it says otherwise.

final_quiz.q: Before your checkride, the owner suggests pulling the stall warning breaker because the horn is annoying in slow flight. The warning is required equipment. What does AC 61-67C say?
options: Fine, as long as you announce it to the examiner
Stall warning devices should not be deactivated for pilot certification flight tests in airplanes that require them
Fine, because the ACS tests only buffet recognition
Fine for commercial tests but not private
final_quiz.why: AC 61-67C says stall warning devices should not be deactivated for pilot certification flight tests in airplanes for which they are required equipment [[13:22|AC 61-67C para 402]].

final_quiz.q: On a short-field takeoff at a high pitch attitude and full power, why is too little right rudder a spin hazard?
options: It raises the stall speed by 40 percent
P-factor yaws the airplane left; with the wing near the critical AOA, uncoordinated flight can lead to a spin
It makes the engine lose power
It moves the CG aft
final_quiz.why: At high AOA the downward-moving blade makes more thrust and yaws the airplane left; wrong rudder makes the flight uncoordinated at the very moment the AOA is high [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

final_quiz.q: At night over dark terrain, a slow roll develops into a descending turn. You notice nothing and take no action. Which type of spatial disorientation does the AFH call this?
options: Recognized spatial disorientation
Unrecognized spatial disorientation
Incapacitating spatial disorientation
Startle response
final_quiz.why: In unrecognized spatial disorientation the pilot is unaware an upset is developing and takes no corrective action [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: Compared with a spin at a sea-level practice area, what does AC 61-67C say about a spin at a high density altitude?
options: Altitude loss will be smaller
Greater altitude losses can be expected
The indicated stall speed doubles
Spins are impossible above 5,000 feet
final_quiz.why: Greater losses can be expected at higher density altitudes [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]]. Indicated stall speed changes little with altitude [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100j]].

final_quiz.q: In a right spin you instinctively hold right aileron (with the spin). What does the AFH say this can do?
options: Stop the rotation faster
Speed up the rotation, steepen the spin attitude and delay recovery
Nothing, because the ailerons are stalled
Turn the spin into a spiral and end it
final_quiz.why: Aileron in the direction of the spin may accelerate the rotation, steepen the spin attitude and delay recovery; neutral ailerons are best [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the official sources the AFH lists for deciding whether an airplane is approved for spins?
options: The Type Certificate Data Sheet or aircraft specifications
The AFM/POH limitations section
A placard in clear view of the pilot
Another pilot's report that the airplane recovers fine
final_quiz.why: The official sources are the TCDS or specifications, the AFM/POH limitations section and the placard [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. The AFH warns about pilots who rationalize ignoring spin restrictions.

final_quiz.q: Your airplane's POH spin recovery differs in one step from the AFH six-step template. Which do you follow?
options: The AFH template, because it is FAA guidance
The POH procedure; the AFH template is for when the manufacturer gives none
Whichever you learned first
The AC 61-67C procedure
final_quiz.why: POH techniques take precedence over the AFH section; use the six-step template only in the absence of the manufacturer's procedure [[24:127|AFH 5-22]] [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

takeaways: No spin without both a stall and yaw: break the stall and stop the yaw.
The descending wing is more stalled; that difference drives autorotation.
Phases: entry, incipient, developed, recovery. Start recovery early, before one full turn.
Recovery: POH first. Otherwise power idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, brisk forward elevator, rudder neutral when rotation stops, gentle pull-out.
Airspeed climbing means spiral, not spin: power off, unload, roll level, then raise the nose.
Aft CG and extra weight make spins easier to enter and harder or impossible to recover; a utility airplane loaded to normal limits may not recover past one turn.
Most accidental spins come from a distracted pilot in an uncoordinated, low, slow turn. Go around instead of skidding.
cfi_notes: The private Task (PA.VII.D) and the commercial Task (CA.VII.E) have identical K, R and Skills text (ACS PA.VII.D; ACS CA.VII.E). Raise the depth for commercial applicants: loading near aft limits with passengers and bags, 91.307 limits with paying passengers, and why utility approval depends on loading.

AFH 5-23 says the first spin turn costs about 1,000 feet and later turns about half that [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]; the AFH's own Figure 5-16 and AC 61-67C give about 500 feet per 3-second turn [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]]. Figure 5-16 also says the incipient phase is about 2 turns and recovery 1/4 to 1/2 turn, while the AFH text says 2 to 4 turns and a quarter turn to several turns [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Present all of these as rough estimates and use the POH or your own airplane's data.

AC 61-67C (2000) says to move the elevator briskly forward 'when the rotation slows', to about neutral [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]]. The AFH says to apply it immediately after full rudder, forward of neutral, without waiting for the rotation to stop [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. On flaps, the AFH says to retract flaps and retractable gear as soon as practicable after spin entry [[24:129|AFH 5-24]], while AC 61-67C para 400a(4) says that in the normal-category certification test the flaps may be retracted during recovery but not before rotation has stopped [[13:21|AC 61-67C para 400]]; one is pilot guidance, the other a test condition. Teach the AFH and the POH; mention the AC wording so students recognize it in older material.

AC 61-67C describes normal, utility and acrobatic spin testing under old sections such as 23.221, 23.807 and 23.1567 [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 108]] [[13:22|AC 61-67C para 400]]. Current Part 23 has one normal category with 'certified for aerobatics' as the dividing line [[60:99|14 CFR 23.2005]] [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. The AFH notes that 23.221(a) still applies to airplanes certified under it [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Most trainers are legacy airplanes, so teach both and always go to the POH and placard.
AC 61-67C para 301 says the 91.307(d) exception covers an ATP instructing under 61.167 [[13:20|AC 61-67C para 301]]. The current rule says 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. Teach the CFR text.

PARE is a widely used instructor memory aid, not an FAA term; it does not appear in any of the FAA sources used for this lesson. It covers only the first four AFH steps; make sure students also say 'neutralize rudder' and 'gentle pull-out', where many secondary stalls happen [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

AC 61-67C's spiral recovery (release back pressure, neutralize rudder, recover from the dive) [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 112]] is shorter than the AFH five-step template that starts with power to idle and unloading before rolling [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Teach the AFH template.

PHAK Figure 5-39 is drawn for shape, not precision: at 60 degrees its stall speed curve reads near 55 percent, while the square-root rule and AC 61-67C give about 40 percent [[13:7|AC 61-67C para 100]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C para 100g]]. Teach the AC numbers and use the chart to show how fast both curves climb past about 50 degrees.

The term 'accelerated spin' is not defined in any of the FAA sources used here. Teach what the sources do say: power and pro-spin aileron speed up rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]], accelerated stalls are usually more severe and often unexpected [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]], and failure to recover from one at once may result in a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
gaps: The actual spin recovery procedure, whether the airplane is approved for spins, and the weight and CG limits for spins come only from your POH/AFM, placards and TCDS [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].
No source here gives altitude loss, turns to recover or spin attitude for a specific training airplane; the AFH and AC numbers are generic estimates.
The sources do not define an 'accelerated spin' or cover inverted spins; ask a CFI with spin experience if you meet those terms.
The sources do not say which way the ball moves for a particular panel layout in a spin, only that it depends on the instrument's location [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

14 CFR 61.125 does not list spin knowledge for commercial applicants, although 61.105(b)(11) does for private [[60:310|14 CFR 61.125]] [[60:296|14 CFR 61.105(b)(11)]]; the commercial requirement comes from this ACS Task. Spin flight training is not required unless you go on to CFI [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183(i)]].

activities.title: Match the spin phase or type
activities.intro: Tap a term, then the description that fits it.

pairs.r: The pilot supplies the stall and the yaw, on purpose or by accident
Stalled and rotating, but forces are not yet in balance
Rotation rate, airspeed and descent rate steady, path nearly vertical
Rotation stops and the AOA drops below critical
Near-level pitch and roll, spin axis near the CG
The descending wing is more stalled, so the rotation keeps feeding itself

activities.title: Put the AFH spin recovery in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Apply and hold full opposite rudder
Apply brisk, positive forward elevator (forward of neutral)
Neutralize the rudder when rotation stops
Apply back elevator to return to level flight and adjust power

activities.title: Spin or spiral dive?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Load factor only slightly above 1 G
Recovery hinges on full opposite rudder
Recovery: unload with some forward elevator, then roll level

activities.title: Work the spin numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Using the AFH rule of thumb, how much altitude does a four-turn spin lose before recovery inputs begin?
items.why: First turn about 1,000 ft, each later turn about half: 1,000 + 500 + 500 + 500 = 2,500 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

items.q: Using the AC 61-67C estimate, how much altitude does a 9-second spin lose?
items.why: About 500 ft per 3-second turn: 9 / 3 = 3 turns, and 3 x 500 = 1,500 ft [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]].

items.q: A spin starts at 3,500 ft AGL. Using the AC 61-67C estimate, how many seconds of spinning would bring you down to 1,500 ft AGL?
items.why: 3,500 - 1,500 = 2,000 ft. 2,000 / 500 = 4 turns. 4 x 3 seconds = 12 seconds [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]]. The 1,500 ft AGL floor is the AFH limit for completing an intentional spin recovery [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

items.q: An acrobatic-category airplane is spun for the full six turns. What is the greatest total number of turns (spin plus recovery) the standard allows?
items.why: It must recover in no more than one and a half additional turns: 6 + 1.5 = 7.5 turns [[13:21|AC 61-67C para 400]] [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]].

items.q: The older normal-category test spin lasts one turn or 3 seconds, whichever takes longer. An airplane takes 2.5 seconds per turn. How many turns does the test spin last?
items.why: One turn takes 2.5 seconds, so 3 seconds is longer. 3 / 2.5 = 1.2 turns, then recovery within one more turn [[13:21|AC 61-67C para 400]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

activities.title: True or false: approvals and rules
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Normal-category airplanes certified under the older 23.221(a) had to show recovery only from a one-turn or 3-second spin.
cards.why: True, unless it showed the optional spin resistance instead. Many were never required to recover from a fully developed spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

cards.s: AC 61-67C says spin training for flight instructor applicants must be done in an aircraft approved for spins.
cards.why: True. Spin training must be accomplished in an aircraft that is approved for spins, after checking the AFM or POH entry and recovery techniques [[13:19|AC 61-67C para 300]].

cards.s: Under current Part 23, an airplane not certified for aerobatics may be used for whip stalls.
cards.why: False. Maneuvers incident to normal flying include stalls, except whip stalls [[60:99|14 CFR 23.2005]].

cards.s: The 91.307 parachute rule does not apply during a practical test for a pilot certificate.
cards.why: True. Flight tests for pilot certification or rating are excepted [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].

cards.s: Commercial pilot applicants must receive spin training and an endorsement.
cards.why: False. Spin training and the endorsement are required for flight instructor airplane and glider applicants [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183(i)]] [[13:19|AC 61-67C para 300]].

cards.s: In an airplane placarded against spins, recovery from a fully developed spin is not assured.
cards.why: True. The pilot should assume it could become uncontrollable [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

activities.title: Read the stall speed and load factor chart
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the chart. Read the shape of the curves; the square-root rule gives the exact numbers.

pins.label: Gentle bank: load factor barely rises
45 degree level bank: stall speed up about one fifth
About 66 degrees of bank: 2.5 G, a typical spin pull-out load
About 75 degrees of bank (4 G): stall speed doubled

activities.title: From preflight to the pattern, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying solo in a four-seat airplane placarded 'No acrobatic maneuvers, including spins, approved.' You plan power-on stall practice well above the ground, then a few landings in a gusty pattern.

steps.s: In a power-on stall at altitude the nose yaws left at the break, the left wing drops past 90 degrees of bank and the airplane starts to rotate left.
options: Hold back pressure and level the wings with right aileron
Spin recovery now: the POH procedure, or power idle, ailerons neutral, full right rudder, brisk forward elevator
Add full power to fly out of it
Let it develop so you can be sure of the direction
steps.why: On recognizing a spin or approaching spin, start recovery immediately [[24:127|AFH 5-22]], before 360 degrees of rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]; use the POH procedure or the AFH template [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

steps.s: As you start the recovery the engine stops and the propeller windmills.
options: Stop the recovery and restart the engine first
Keep flying the spin recovery; AC 61-67C says to assume power may not be available in a spin
Full throttle to restart it before anything else
Hold full back elevator to slow the descent
steps.why: Centrifugal force on the fuel can interrupt it and stop the engine in a spin, so assume power is not available [[13:13|AC 61-67C para 111]]. Power is not part of the recovery anyway: step 1 is idle [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

steps.s: The rotation stops. The nose is well down, the rudder is still fully deflected and the airspeed is climbing.
options: Keep the rudder in and pull hard to level
Neutralize the rudder, then pull back smoothly to level flight within G limits
Push further forward to gain more speed
Add full power before doing anything else
steps.why: Neutralize the rudder when rotation stops, then apply back pressure to level flight without overdoing it, or risk a secondary stall [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

steps.s: Back at the airport, the wind is gusting and there is a strong crosswind on final.
options: Fly the normal approach speed exactly
Use a higher than normal approach speed
Fly slower than normal to land short
Use full flaps and the slowest safe speed
steps.why: Gusts can raise the AOA suddenly and stall the airplane at a higher airspeed; in moderate to severe turbulence or strong crosswinds, keep a higher than normal approach speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C para 100l]].
